title: Arterial (ischaemic) leg ulcer
summary: Punched-out, painful, distal ulcers from peripheral arterial disease. Never compress an ischaemic limb; refer urgently to vascular, same day for critical limb ischaemia.

what: An **arterial ulcer** is skin loss caused by tissue **ischaemia** from peripheral arterial disease. It accounts for about 10–20% of leg ulcers, alone or mixed with venous disease.
cause: Atherosclerosis (or embolism) reduces flow, so poorly perfused sites become necrotic after minor trauma. Risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, CKD and age.

list: Site: toes, heel, bony prominences, lateral malleolus, shin.
Pain often **severe**, worse on elevation and at night (eased by hanging the leg out of bed).
Foot: cold, pale or mottled, shiny, hairless, weak or absent pulses; dependent rubor; **claudication**.
Examine pulses and measure **ABPI** (or TBPI in diabetes, where calcified vessels give falsely high ABPI).
Urgent vascular assessment (duplex, angiography) for critical limb ischaemia.

differentials: [Venous leg ulcer](condition:venous-leg-ulcer) (gaiter area, shallow, exudative), [diabetic foot ulcer](condition:diabetic-foot-ulcer), pressure ulcer, [pyoderma gangrenosum](condition:pyoderma-gangrenosum), vasculitis, malignancy.

list: Urgent **vascular referral**, especially with rest pain, gangrene or critical ischaemia.
Risk factors: stop smoking, antiplatelet and statin therapy (NICE CG147 and vascular advice); optimise blood pressure and diabetes.
Analgesia, and wound care directed by tissue viability or vascular.

red_flags: **Critical limb ischaemia:** rest pain, gangrene, tissue loss, or a cold pulseless foot: **same-day vascular**.
Acute limb ischaemia (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishingly cold): emergency.
pearls: **Any leg ulcer may be mixed.** Always assess the arterial supply before compression.
Painful ulcer worse on elevation suggests arterial.
